title: 03: Significance tests
text:
This week, you’ll revisit the same model you fit last week, focusing now on manually recreating the significance tests reported in summary(). You’ll also practice writing up the model results using APA-style reporting.






NoteGet set up




Open RStudio.
Create a new R Markdown (.Rmd) file for this week’s exercises.
Save it somewhere you can find it again.
Give it a clear name (for example, dapr2_lab03.Rmd).
In the first code chunk, load the packages you’ll need this week (and install them if you don’t have them already):

tidyverse






Research question (RQ): Is there an association between wellbeing and time spent outdoors, when controlling for the effect that social interaction has on wellbeing?
Data dictionary:








variable
description




age
Age in years of respondent


outdoor_time
Self report estimated number of hours per week spent outdoors


social_int
Self report estimated number of social interactions per week (both online and in-person)


routine
Binary 1=Yes/0=No response to the question 'Do you follow a daily routine throughout the week?'


wellbeing
Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Wellbeing Scale (WEMWBS), a self-report measure of mental health and wellbeing. The scale is scored by summing responses to each item, with items answered on a 1 to 5 Likert scale. The minimum scale score is 14 and the maximum is 70


location
Location of primary residence (City, Suburb, Rural)


steps_k
Average weekly number of steps in thousands (as given by activity tracker if available)













NoteMore detail about this dataset





From the Edinburgh & Lothians, 100 city/suburb residences and 100 rural residences were chosen at random and contacted to participate in the study. The Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Wellbeing Scale (WEMWBS) was used to measure mental health and wellbeing.
Participants filled out a questionnaire including items concerning: estimated average number of hours spent outdoors each week, estimated average number of social interactions each week (whether on-line or in-person), whether a daily routine is followed (yes/no). For those respondents who had an activity tracker app or smart watch, they were asked to provide their average weekly number of steps.





Recap from last week


Question 1


Read in the data from https://uoepsy.github.io/data/wellbeing_rural.csv and store it in a variable named mwdata (“mw” stands for “mental wellbeing”).
Using the function lm(), fit the linear model represented by the mathematical model formulation below, and name the result mdl.
\[
\text{wellbeing} = \beta_0 +
(\beta_1 \cdot \text{outdoor\_time}) +
(\beta_2 \cdot \text{social\_int}) +
\epsilon
\]




 Solution 


Solution 1. 

mwdata <- read_csv("https://uoepsy.github.io/data/wellbeing_rural.csv")
mdl    <- lm(wellbeing ~ outdoor_time + social_int, data = mwdata)






Test significance of \(\beta_1\)


Question 2


Our RQ is interested in the association between hours spent outdoors and wellbeing, holding social interaction constant. Thus the coefficient we’re interested in testing for this RQ is \(\beta_1\). \(\beta_1\) represents the slope over the predictor variable outdoor_time, holding the other predictor variable social_int constant.
We’ll start by defining our null hypothesis H0 and our alternative hypothesis H1 for the significance test for \(\beta_1\).

Write a sentence in plain English that states the null hypothesis that we’ll test for \(\beta_1\).
Then write another sentence that states the alternative hypothesis for \(\beta_1\).
Finally, write the null and alternative hypotheses again, this time using mathematical notation.


🗂️ See Specifying hypotheses flash card.





 Solution 


Solution 2. In plain English:

The null hypothesis is that \(\beta_1\) is equal to zero (in other words, that the slope over outdoor_time is zero, or that the line that associates outdoor_time with wellbeing, while holding social_int constant, is flat).
The alternative hypothesis is that \(\beta_1\) is not equal to zero.


\[
\begin{align}
H_0 &: \beta_1 = 0 \\
H_1 &: \beta_1 \neq 0\\
\end{align}
\]
Write:
$$
\begin{align}
H_0 &: \beta_1 = 0 \\
H_1 &: \beta_1 \neq 0\\
\end{align}
$$





Question 3


Run the code summary(mdl) to produce the model summary.
Write down the observed t-statistic for \(\beta_1\).
(Which coefficient maps to \(\beta_1\)? Recall that \(\beta_1\) is the slope over outdoor_time, which is represented in the model summary as the value in the Estimate column for outdoor_time.)












 Solution 


Solution 3. 

summary(mdl)


Call:
lm(formula = wellbeing ~ outdoor_time + social_int, data = mwdata)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-15.7611  -3.1308  -0.4213   3.3126  18.8406 

Coefficients:
             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  28.62018    1.48786  19.236  < 2e-16 ***
outdoor_time  0.19909    0.05060   3.935 0.000115 ***
social_int    0.33488    0.08929   3.751 0.000232 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 5.065 on 197 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.1265,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.1176 
F-statistic: 14.26 on 2 and 197 DF,  p-value: 1.644e-06



\(\beta_1\) is the coefficient for outdoor_time, so the observed t-statistic is 3.935.












Question 4


To find out whether this t-statistic is significantly different from zero, we must compare it to a t-distribution with the appropriate number of degrees of freedom. The “appropriate” degrees of freedom are determined based on the data and the model. In this question, you’ll work out what that quantity should be.
The t-distribution will have degrees of freedom equal to \(n - k - 1\), where

\(n\) = sample size, i.e., number of observations
\(k\) = number of predictors, i.e., number of \(\beta\) coefficients not including the intercept

Figure out the values for \(n\) and \(k\). Use them to calculate how many degrees of freedom this coefficient’s t-distribution should have.




 Solution 


Solution 4. In mwdata, we have one observation per row. So to work out \(n\), we can look at the number of observations in the RStudio environment, or alternatively:

nrow(mwdata)

[1] 200



The model has two predictors, so \(k = 2\).
Thus:
\[
\begin{align}
df &= n - k - 1 \\
  &= 200 - 2 - 1 \\
  &= 197
\end{align}
\]





Question 5


Assume \(\alpha = .05\) (the standard in Psychology) and a two-tailed test.
Copy the code below. It uses qt() to find the critical t-values (that is, the t-values which establish the boundaries for statistical significance) on the t-distribution with the appropriate degrees of freedom.
Replace ... with the degrees of freedom you determined in Q4.
Then run the code.

c(
  lower = round(qt(0.025, ...), 3),
  upper = round(qt(0.975, ...), 3)
)

Write down your answer: Does the observed t-value for \(\beta_1\) fall beyond these critical values? Can we reject the H0?

🗂️ See Reconstructing model estimates > t value flash card.





 Solution 


Solution 5. If our observed t-value for \(\beta_1\) is smaller than –1.972 or greater than 1.972, then we conclude that \(\beta_1\) is significantly different from zero.
Our observed t-value is 3.935, which is greater than 1.972. Thus \(\beta_1\) is significantly different from zero, and we can reject the H0.





Variance explained


Question 6


All model summaries present two \(R^2\) values, one unadjusted and one adjusted.
Write down your answer: For this model, which one should we pay attention to? Why?
Then write down your answer: How much variance in wellbeing scores does our model explain?

🗂️ See Assessing model fit > R-squared and adjusted R-squared flash card.





 Solution 


Solution 6. The model summary presents both “Multiple R-squared” and “Adjusted R-squared”.
Multiple \(R^2\) is appropriate for linear models with one single predictor. Adjusted \(R^2\) is appropriate for linear models with more than one predictor. We should therefore pay attention to the adjusted \(R^2\).
Why is \(R^2\) appropriate for LMs with more than one predictor? Because we will always be able to explain the data better if we add in more predictors. This means that multiple \(R^2\) will always increase, the more predictors we add. To take this into account, adjusted \(R^2\) modifies this value depending on how many predictors the model contains.

Question 7


Imagine you’re writing a brief explanation of your analysis for one of your colleagues who’s not in this lab. Your goal is for somebody else to be able to reproduce the exact same analysis that you ran, based only on the information in your description.

the structure of your model (what’s the outcome? what are the predictors?).

(We know this is a challenging task, but do your best—and we’ll practice this more in weeks to come. You’ll be writing descriptions like this in all your future reports.)




 Solution 


Solution 7. We ran a multiple linear regression model to predict people’s WEMWBS wellbeing score as a function of how many hours they spend outdoors per week as well as how many social interactions they have per week.





Question 8


Write a sentence to explain to yourself what the outdoor_time coefficient in the model summary means.
Write another sentence to state whether you can or cannot reject the H0 you defined above.

🗂️ See Multiple regression > Interpreting results flash card.





 Solution 


Solution 8. Holding the number of social interactions constant, increasing one hour of outdoor time is associated with an increase of 0.20 points on the WEMWBS scale.
The result is statistically significant, so yes, we can reject H0.
(Note: the coefficient interpretation is only complete if it mentions holding the other predictor(s) constant.)





Question 9


The APA has official guidelines on how to report regression coefficient estimates. Use this template structure:

(Tip: use confint(mdl) to get each coefficient’s 95% CI.)
Here’s an example of how to include this information in a sentence:

The slope was significantly different from zero (\(b\) = 0.54, 95% CI [0.32, 0.76], \(p\) = .041). I therefore reject the H0 that this estimate is equal to zero.

When reporting the p-value, you should report exact p-values to three decimal places, with no zero in front of the decimal, for example: \(p\) = .041 or \(p\) = .222. However, if \(p\) is smaller than .001, just write \(p\) < .001.

🗂️ See the APA Numbers and Statistics Guide.





 Solution 


Solution 9.

(Intercept)  25.69  31.55
outdoor_time  0.10   0.30

According to the model, increasing one hour of outdoor time is associated with an increase of 0.20 points on the WEMWBS scale, while holding the number of social interactions constant. This estimate is significantly different from zero (\(b\) = 0.20, 95% CI [0.10, 0.30], \(p\) < .001), and we can therefore reject the H0.





Bonus conceptual question


Question 10


You’ll notice that in the model summary, all \(\beta\) coefficients (intercept AND slopes) are associated with a t-value and a p-value. The H0 being tested for all of these parameters is that their estimates are equal to zero.
This H0 makes a lot of sense for the slope coefficients: if a slope is equal to zero, then the line is flat. When the line is flat, there’s no association between \(x\) and \(y\).
In this question, we want you to ask yourself, and write down your thinking: To what extent does this H0 also make sense for the intercept? If our intercept estimate is significantly different from zero, does that tell us anything interesting? Are values of zero even possible for the intercept of this model?
If you like thinking visually, you might find it helpful to recreate the model-fitted plot from last week using the following code:

    mdl, 
    type = 'eff', 
    terms = c(
        'outdoor_time', 
        'social_int'
    ),
    show.data = TRUE
)





 Solution 


Solution 10. The H0 for the intercept is that its estimate is equal to zero. In other words, that the average estimated outcome value, when all predictors are equal to zero, is zero.
This is usually not really a plausible or interesting H0, and it’s definitely not plausible for our wellbeing example! We’d never actually expect wellbeing scores to be equal to zero. All the scores we observe are between 22 and 59, and the range of all possible values is 14 to 70. Zero isn’t even a possibility!
So when the significance test for the intercept tells us that our intercept estimate is significantly different from zero, it’s like … thanks I guess? We didn’t really think it was going to be equal to zero anyway.
In short: Comparing the intercept coefficient to zero is not really that informative or interesting when we have a continuous outcome variable that we’d expect to be different from zero anyway. The intercept will almost always be significantly different from zero, and we don’t usually care.

text:
This week (and every fifth week this year), you’ll practice writing up the analysis that was developed live during lectures.
Your goal is to present your analysis in a journal-article-style Results section that a reader could reproduce in any statistical software, not just R.
Quick links to key flash cards:

🗂️ Analysis workflow (Block 1)
🗂️ Reporting LM analysis checklist







Important



The example write-ups that will be provided on Friday are not perfect.
You must not copy them directly for this write-up or any future assessment, as copying and presenting them as your own work would constitute academic misconduct. But you may refer to them for stylistic guidance.








NoteGet set up




Open RStudio.
Create a new R Markdown (.Rmd) file for this week’s exercises.
Save it somewhere you can find it again.
Give it a clear name (for example, dapr2_lab05.Rmd).
In the first code chunk, load the packages you’ll need this week (and install them if you don’t have them already):

tidyverse
psych
sjPlot
kableExtra
patchwork






The data in FOMOdataset.csv contain eight attributes collected from a sample of \(n=3370\) hypothetical individuals across the UK, and include:








Variable
Description




FOMO

Age

N

NoteMore detail about this dataset





The data used for this write-up exercise are simulated, drawing on recent work on Fear of Missing Out (FOMO), socio-demographic factors, and the Big Five personality traits. The simulated data are based on the findings of this work, and acted to expand upon the methods and results reported in the following paper:
Rozgonjuk, D., Sindermann, C., Elhai, J. D., & Montag, C. (2021). Individual differences in Fear of Missing Out (FOMO): Age, gender, and the Big Five personality trait domains, facets, and items. Personality and Individual Differences, 171, 110546. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.paid.2020.110546
In the current study, participants were invited to an online study investigating the associations among FOMO, socio-demographic factors, and personality. The final sample comprised 3370 people. Participants completed a FOMO scale and a personality inventory. The 10-item FOMO scale measured the extent of experiencing apprehension regarding missing out on interesting events of others on a 5-point scale (1 = “not at all true of me” to 5 = “extremely true of me”), producing a possible range of scores between 10 and 50. The Big Five Inventory (BFI) is a 45-item personality assessment questionnaire (note that only 44 items were used to match the study above) that uses a five-point response scale (1 = “very inapplicable” to 5 = “very applicable”). The BFI consists of five domains: Neuroticism (8 items; possible range of scores 8-40), Extraversion (8 items; possible range of scores 8-40), Openness to Experience (10 items; possible range of scores 10-50), Agreeableness (9 items; possible range of scores 9-45), and Conscientiousness (9 items; possible range of scores 9-45). We extended the aforementioned study to include an extra socio-demographic variable - a measure of popularity on social media based on the number of followers. Unlike the original study, we do not have measures of gender, education level, or specific country of residence.





RQ1

RQ: How is people’s sense of Fear of Missing Out (FOMO) associated with their age and how many Instagram followers they have?
Specific predictions:

As age increases, FOMO will decrease.
As the number of Instagram followers increases, FOMO will increase.








TipProvided analysis code for RQ1





This code should resemble the analysis developed during lectures this week.

# RQ1 example code ----

# Follows workflow here: dapr2/2627/dapr2_flashcards/resources/workflow.html

## Phase 1: Before model fitting ----

### 1a: Set up code and data ----

# Load required R packages
library(tidyverse)   # for wrangling
library(psych)       # for summarising
library(sjPlot)      # for nice tables/plots
library(kableExtra)  # for nicely-formatted tables
library(patchwork)   # for combining plots into one graphic


# Read in data
fomo <- read_csv("https://uoepsy.github.io/data/FOMOdataset.csv")


# Tidy data if needed
glimpse(fomo)  # all numeric, so we'll use psych::describe() to look for weird data
describe(fomo)  # min and max look reasonable
table(is.na(fomo))  # no NAs
# good to continue!

### 1b: Set up the variables we'll model ----

# RQ: How is people's sense of Fear of Missing Out (FOMO) associated with their age and how many Instagram followers they have?

# Based on RQ, identify outcome variables and predictors.
# - Outcome: `FOMO`
# - Predictors: `Age`, `TotalFollowers`

# Based on RQ, decide whether to test hypotheses using coefficient significance tests or model comparison.
# - The RQ is about associations between variables, so we'll test it using significance test for coef estimates.

# Set up continuous predictors. (e.g., any transformations?)
# - One option might be to z-score Age and TotalFollowers.
#   This would be an important step if Age = 0 and TotalFollowers = 0 were totally meaningless quantities (imagine Height = 0 or ShoeSize = 0 – impossible and nonexistent).
#   But Age = 0 means an infant, and TotalFollowers = 0 means someone with no followers.
#   So they are reasonable quantities to generate predictions for.

# Explore patterns in the data by plotting outcome and predictor variables together.

p_age <- fomo |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Age, y = FOMO)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = 'lm', se = FALSE)
p_age

p_followers <- fomo |>
  ggplot(aes(x = TotalFollowers, y = FOMO)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = 'lm', se = FALSE)
p_followers

p_age + p_followers  # combine using patchwork



## Phase 2: Model fitting ----

# Write the mathematical model formulation for your model(s).
#  $$
#    \text{FOMO} = \beta_0 + (\beta_1 \cdot \text{Age}) + (\beta_2 \cdot \text{Followers}) + \epsilon
#  $$


# Explicitly define the hypotheses that your RQ is aiming to test.
#  $$
#  \begin{align}
#  H_0 &: \text{ All } \beta_j = 0 \text{ for } j = 1, 2 \\
#  H_1 &: \text{ Any } \beta_j \neq 0 \\
#  \end{align}
#  $$

# Fit your model(s) using lm().
m1 <- lm(
  FOMO ~ Age + TotalFollowers,
  data = fomo
)


## Phase 3: After model fitting ----

### 3a: Plot and interpret model estimates ----

# Interpret the coefficient estimates (if appropriate for your RQ).
summary(m1)
confint(m1) |> round(2)
confint(m1) |> round(3)  # for TotalFollowers

# - `Intercept`: The estimated FOMO score for someone aged zero with zero total followers is 26.52 points.
# - `Age`: Increasing one year of age is associated with a decrease in FOMO score of 0.17 points (holding follower count constant). This estimate is significantly different from zero (b = –0.17, 95% CI [–0.18, –0.15], p < .001).
# - prediction supported!
#   - `TotalFollowers`: Increasing one follower is associated with an increase in FOMO score of 0.018 points (holding age constant). This estimate is significantly different from zero (b = 0.018, 95% CI [0.016, 0.020], p < .001).
# - prediction supported!
#   - (rounded to 3 dp because otherwise estim and CI bounds are all 0.02)


# Generate a nicely-formatted regression table (if appropriate for your RQ).
tab_model(
  m1,
  dv.labels = 'Fear of missing out (FOMO)',
  pred.labels = c("Age" = "Age (in years)"),
  title = "RQ1: Linear model coefficient estimates"
)

# Plot model-fitted values (if appropriate for your RQ).
plot_model(
  m1, 
  type = 'eff', 
  terms = c('Age', 'TotalFollowers'), 
  show.data = TRUE
)






Question 1


Set the scene (so the reader knows what you’re talking about).

Remind the reader briefly what the study aimed to test (e.g., what the predictions were).





 Solution example


Solution 1. In this study, we wanted to test how people’s Fear of Missing Out (FOMO) is associated with socio-demographic factors: specifically, people’s age and how many followers they have on Instagram. We predicted that as age increases, FOMO will decrease, but that as the number of followers increases, FOMO will increase.





Question 2


Describe and show the sample data (so that the reader knows how generalisable your analysis might be).

Introduce the variables the study is using to test this prediction, but avoid using R variable names; describe the variables in human-readable terms instead (e.g., what scale are they on? how were they measured?)

Solution 2. To test these predictions, we are using data gathered from 3370 individuals across the UK. The data contains a FOMO score, as measured by a 10-item FOMO scale which produces scores ranging from 10 to 50. The data also contains each respondent’s age in years and the number of Instagram followers they have.





Question 3


Visualise and summarise data patterns that address the RQ (so the reader knows the basic pattern of what you found).

Include a plot of the data which includes all relevant variables (and make sure to refer to it in the text).

Tip: If you transform any continuous predictors for analysis, use the transformed version of the predictor in the plot.

In a sentence or two, describe the overall pattern of results.

Tip: No inferential stats have been done yet, so we can’t make any claims just yet about whether the predictions were supported. But it is OK to say whether the results appear broadly in line with the prediction.






 Solution example


Solution 3. As shown in Figure 1, age appears to be negatively associated with FOMO (left), while number of Instagram followers appears positively associated with FOMO (right).

Question 4


Introduce your statistical analysis (so the reader can interpret the numbers you will report).

State that you’re running your analysis using R, and cite the developers (run citation() in the console to get the citation for your version of R).
State the \(\alpha\) level that you’re using for all your analyses (in Psychology, the convention is 5%).
Describe the structure of your model in words, e.g.: “We fit a linear model predicting Y as a function of X1 and X2”.
If continuous predictors have been transformed, describe the transformation, e.g.: “X2 has been z-scored”.
Include the mathematical model formulation of your model.
Explain the hypotheses that your analysis will test and include them in mathematical notation.





 Solution example


Solution 4. We conducted all statistical analyses using R (R Core Team, 2025), and we will consider effects significant at \(\alpha = .05\).
To address the RQ, we fit a linear model which predicts FOMO as a function of age and number of Instagram followers. The mathematical model formulation is as follows:
\[
\text{FOMO} = \beta_0 + (\beta_1 \cdot \text{Age}) + (\beta_2 \cdot \text{Followers}) + \epsilon
\]
The null hypothesis is that neither age nor number of followers are significantly associated with FOMO. And the alternative hypothesis is that either age or number of followers, or both, are significantly associated with FOMO:
\[
\begin{align}
H_0 &: \text{ All } \beta_j = 0 \text{ for } j = 1, 2 \\
H_1 &: \text{ Any } \beta_j \neq 0 \\
\end{align}
\]





Question 5


Report the results of your analysis (so the reader knows exactly what you found).

State which model coefficient(s) are related to which prediction(s), and what direction/sign (positive or negative) you would expect the coefficients to have if the predictions were supported, if applicable.
State the key coefficient estimates along with their 95% CI and p-value, e.g.: “The slope associating X1 and Y was significantly different from zero (\(b\) = 0.26, 95% CI [0.23, 0.29], \(p\) < 0.001)” or “The slope associating X1 and Y was not significantly different from zero (\(b\) = 0.26, 95% CI [–0.04, 0.56], \(p\) = 0.18)”, if applicable.

Tip: You don’t need to report every single parameter estimate. Focus on the one(s) you identified as being relevant to your prediction(s).

The function tab_model() from the package sjPlot may be useful here, but note that tab_model() causes Rmd files to fail to knit to PDF, so you might want to manually recreate the table it produces.
Plot the model-fitted values (and refer to the plot in the text), if applicable.
Report the results of a model comparison, if applicable.
Report any other information you consider important for your story!





 Solution example


Solution 5. If our predictions were supported, we would expect \(\beta_1\) (the slope coefficient for age) to be negative, and we would expect \(\beta_2\) (the slope coefficient for the number of followers) to be positive.
Indeed, \(\beta_1\) is negative and significantly different from zero (\(b\) = –0.17, 95% CI [–0.18, –0.15], \(p\) < .001). Thus age is significantly negatively associated with FOMO: for every year increased in age (holding follower count constant), FOMO is estimated to decrease by 0.17 points. Further, \(\beta_2\) is positive and also significantly different from zero (\(b\) = 0.018, 95% CI [0.016, 0.020], \(p\) < .001), indicating that follower count is significantly positively associated with FOMO. Specifically, for an increase in one follower (holding age constant), FOMO is estimated to increase by 0.018 points. Thus our predictions are both supported and we can reject the null hypothesis defined above.

 Solution example: full write-up for RQ1


Solution 6. The data also contains each respondent’s age in years and the number of Instagram followers they have.
As shown in Figure 1, age appears to be negatively associated with FOMO (left), while number of Instagram followers appears positively associated with FOMO (right).





Figure 1: Associations between socio-demographic factors and FOMO. Age appears to have a positive association with FOMO, while the number of instagram followers appears to have a negative association, in line with predictions.





We conducted all statistical analyses using R (R Core Team, 2025), and we will consider effects significant at \(\alpha = .05\).
To address the RQ, we fit a linear model which predicts FOMO as a function of age and number of Instagram followers. The mathematical model formulation is as follows:
\[
\text{FOMO} = \beta_0 + (\beta_1 \cdot \text{Age}) + (\beta_2 \cdot \text{Followers}) + \epsilon

\[
\begin{align}
H_0 &: \text{ All } \beta_j = 0 \text{ for } j = 1, 2 \\
H_1 &: \text{ Any } \beta_j \neq 0 \\
\end{align}
\]
If our predictions were supported, we would expect \(\beta_1\) (the slope coefficient for age) to be negative, and we would expect \(\beta_2\) (the slope coefficient for the number of followers) to be positive.
Indeed, \(\beta_1\) is negative and significantly different from zero (\(b\) = –0.17, 95% CI [–0.18, –0.15], \(p\) < .001). Thus age is significantly negatively associated with FOMO: for every year increased in age (holding follower count constant), FOMO is estimated to decrease by 0.17 points. Further, \(\beta_2\) is positive and also significantly different from zero (\(b\) = 0.018, 95% CI [0.016, 0.020], \(p\) < .001), indicating that follower count is significantly positively associated with FOMO. Specifically, for an increase in one follower (holding age constant), FOMO is estimated to increase by 0.018 points. Thus our predictions are both supported and we can reject the null hypothesis defined above.

Common problems in LM write-ups
Below are some examples of common problems we encounter in write-ups of LM analyses. If you want to produce a really clear and strong write-up, then try to avoid these issues. Do any of them appear in the draft you’ve written? If they do, can you edit your draft to solve each one?
Our example solutions, which illustrate how you might get around these problems, will be shared on Friday.






ImportantIncluding too little necessary information





For example:

The first slope was significant (\(b\) = –0.17, 95% CI [–0.18, –0.15], \(p\) < .001). The second slope was also significant (\(b\) = 0.018, 95% CI [0.016, 0.020], \(p\) < .001).


The reader doesn’t know which one is the slope over age and which is the slope over the number of Instagram followers.
The reader also doesn’t know what these numbers mean in the context of the analysis. To remedy this, each coefficient must be interpreted in the context of the data (e.g., something like “holding [other variable] constant, increasing one unit of [this variable] is associated with an increase/decrease in [outcome] of [x] points”).


For example:

Figure 1: Plot of the data


What are the variables being plotted?
What patterns/associations should the reader notice in the plot?
General figure caption advice: If you were describing this plot in words to somebody who cannot see it, what would you say?










ImportantIncluding too much unnecessary detail





For example:

There are 3370 rows in the dataframe, and each row represents one participant. There was no data cleaning / outlier removal / transformations.”


The first sentence is all right, but it could be easily shortened to “We have data from 3370 participants”, which is what we actually care about more than the number of rows in the dataframe.
If a particular analysis step is not applicable, then you don’t need to mention that you didn’t do it.


For example:

The predictions were supported. \(\beta_0\) shows that the estimated mean FOMO score for people aged zero with no followers is 26.52 points. \(\beta_1\) shows […]


The intercept \(\beta_0\) was not involved in any of our predictions, so you don’t need to spend your valuable word count on reporting it in a sentence. It’ll appear anyway in the regression coefficient table, so the readers will still see what it is, and they can interpret it themselves if they want to.










ImportantUsing R variable names and R notation in the text





For example:

The dataset contains the variables FOMO, Age, TotalFollowers, N, E, O, A, and C.


Describe in natural English / human-readable language what the variables mean, not what they’re called in our specific dataset.
Your goal is to describe the dataset so that somebody who doesn’t have access to it could, in principle, collect data on the exact same variables.


For example:

The model is FOMO ~ Age + TotalFollowers.


Write out the model structure in words and mathematical notation, not R syntax.
Your goal is to be able to convey the model’s structure even to readers who are using statistical software that is not R.










ImportantUninformative or inaccessible colour in plots





For example:


Code
p_age <- fomo |>  
    ggplot(aes(x = Age, y = FOMO)) +  
    geom_point(colour="limegreen") 
p_followers <- fomo |>  
    ggplot(aes(x = TotalFollowers, y = FOMO)) +  
    geom_point(colour="limegreen")

p_age + p_followers










Bright neon colours are generally to be avoided in scientific plots because many people find them hard to look at.
There’s no reason for both of these plots to have any particular colour, since typically we want to use colour to distinguish different variables or different values of the same variable.


For example:


Code

    ggplot(aes(x = Age, y = FOMO)) +  
    geom_point(colour="limegreen") 
p_followers <- fomo |>  
    ggplot(aes(x = TotalFollowers, y = FOMO)) +  
    geom_point(colour="tomato")

p_age + p_followers










Now we have different colours for each variable, which is fine, but these particular colours (green and red) are a problem for many people who are colourblind and cannot easily distinguish them. Here’s a link to a colourblind-friendly colour palette.










ImportantRepeating the same information in more than one place





For example, including both a plot like this and a table like the one below it:

desc_FOMO <- ggplot(fomo, aes(y=FOMO))+  
  geom_boxplot()

The table also shows some issues with rounding, which we’ll mention as well the next box down.

For example:

It’s hard to correctly read numbers that contain a lot of decimal values, so it’s best to round all your numbers to two decimal places (or three places for p-values).
Also, the p-value column rounds everything to 0—sort of the opposite problem, and also definitely not what we want!
In this case, a better alternative to results$coefficients |> kable() would probably be to manually create a data frame that contains the numbers you want to display.










ImportantHard-to-read “academic” writing style





For example:

In the present study, an analysis was undertaken to examine the association between individuals’ Fear of Missing Out (FOMO), the age of these individuals, and the quantity of followers that they possess on Instagram. It was predicted that the occurrence of an increase in age would be accompanied by the observation of a reduction in FOMO. Additionally, the prediction was made that an increase in the number of followers would occur alongside the observation of an increase in FOMO.


Please, we beg, don’t worry about “sounding academic”! The more naturally you write, the easier it will be for your reader to understand you.
It’s okay (even good!) to write sentences that use “we” or “I” and that describe the actions you took.
Compare the writing above to easier-to-understand sentences like the following:

“In this study, we wanted to find out how FOMO is associated with people’s age and how many followers they have on Instagram.”
“We predicted that as age increases, FOMO will decrease.”











ImportantDrawing over-confident conclusions





For example:

The predictions were correct.


The hypothesis was verified.


Our research question was confirmed.


Statistics cannot tell us whether things are correct or verified or confirmed.
The best we can do, for a prediction, is tell whether it’s supported or not.
And for hypotheses, we can only ever reject the null hypothesis; we never accept or verify the alternative hypothesis.
And our research question just is. We don’t confirm it or reject it, we just do our best to address it.






Bonus challenge: RQ2

RQ: Do the Big 5 personality traits significantly predict FOMO, in addition to the effects of age and total Instagram followers?







TipProvided analysis code for RQ2





This code should resemble the analysis developed during lectures this week.

## Phase 1: Before model fitting ----

### 1a: Set up code and data – DONE ----

### 1b: Set up the variables we'll model ----

  ) |>

## Phase 2: Model fitting ----

# Write the mathematical model formulation for your model(s).
# - First model = model from RQ1. Second model:

# Fit your model(s) using lm().
m2 <- lm(
  FOMO ~ Age + TotalFollowers + O + C + E + A + N,
  data = fomo
)

## Phase 3: After model fitting ----

### 3a: Plot and interpret model estimates ----

Remind the reader briefly what the study aimed to test (e.g., what the predictions were).

Question 9


Introduce your statistical analysis (so the reader can interpret the numbers you will report).

State that you’re running your analysis using R, and cite the developers (run citation() in the console to get the citation for your version of R).
State the \(\alpha\) level that you’re using for all your analyses (in Psychology, the convention is 5%).
Describe the structure of your model in words, e.g.: “We fit a linear model predicting Y as a function of X1, X2, and their interaction”.

Solution 10. To address this research question, we conducted an incremental F-test to compare the model from RQ1 to a new model which contains those same variables as well as each of the Big 5 traits. Specifically, the new model is the following:
\[
\text{FOMO} = \beta_0 +
(\beta_1 \cdot \text{Age}) +
(\beta_2 \cdot \text{Followers}) +

Question 10


Report the results of your analysis (so the reader knows exactly what you found).

State which model coefficient(s) are related to which prediction(s), and what direction/sign (positive or negative) you would expect the coefficients to have if the predictions were supported, if applicable.

Solution 12. Additionally, we are interested in the additional role that personality factors may play in predicting FOMO. Specifically, we want to know: Do the Big 5 personality traits predict FOMO, over and above the roles played by age and number of Instagram followers?

(\beta_1 \cdot \text{Age}) +

(\beta_4 \cdot \text{C}) +
(\beta_5 \cdot \text{E}) +
(\beta_6 \cdot \text{A}) +
(\beta_7 \cdot \text{N}) +
\epsilon
\]

title: 07: Sum coding
text:
This week, you’ll run an analysis using a three-level sum-coded categorical predictor, while also controlling for a continuous numeric covariate.






NoteGet set up




Open RStudio.
Create a new .Rmd file for this week’s exercises.
Save it somewhere you can find it again.
Give it a clear name (for example, dapr2_lab07.Rmd).
In the first code chunk, load the packages you’ll need this week (and install them if you don’t have them already):

tidyverse






RQ: Controlling for people’s pre-existing anxiety levels, is coughing before a lie detector test significantly associated with a lower-than-average heart rate during the test? (Apparently coughing is a way to immediately lower heart rate!)
Data dictionary:








variable
description




age
Age of participant (years)


anx
Anxiety measure (z-scored)


strategy
Pre-test calming strategy (CloseEyes, Cough, DeepBreath)


hr
Average heart rate (in bpm, beats per minute) during test













NoteMore detail about this dataset





Law enforcement in some countries regularly rely on ‘polygraph’ tests as a form of ‘lie detection’. These tests involve measuring heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate and sweat. However, there is very little evidence to suggest that these methods are remotely accurate in being able to determine whether or not someone is lying.
Researchers are interested in if peoples’ heart rates during polygraph tests can be influenced by various pre-test strategies, including deep breathing, or closing their eyes. They recruited 142 participants (ages 22 to 64). Participants were told they were playing a game in which their task was to deceive the lie detector test, and they would receive financial rewards if they managed successfully. At the outset of the study, they completed a questionnaire which asked about their anxiety in relation to taking part. Participants then chose one of three strategies to prepare themselves for the test, each lasting one minute. These were “deep breathing”, “close your eyes”, or “cough”. Then the average heart rate of each participant was recorded during their lie detector test.





Set up and plot data


Question 1


Read in the data from https://uoepsy.github.io/data/polygraph.csv and store it in a variable named heartrate.




 Solution 


Solution 1. 

heartrate <- read_csv('https://uoepsy.github.io/data/polygraph.csv')






Question 2


Make a violin plot (including jittered points and group means) to show the distribution of heart rate hr values for each pre-test calming strategy.

🗂️ See Exploring data visually > Violin plot flash card.





 Solution 


Solution 2. 

heartrate |>
  ggplot(aes(x = strategy, y = hr, fill = strategy, colour = strategy)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_jitter(height = 0, alpha = 0.5) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = 'point', colour = 'black', size = 3) +
  theme(legend.position = 'none') +
  labs(
    y = 'Heart rate (bpm)',
    x = 'Calming strategy'
  )













Set up sum coding


Question 3


First, convert strategy into a factor (don’t worry about ordering levels of the factor).






TipCode hint





For a dataframe df with a column called variable, the following code will take that column and change it into a factor.

df <- df |>
  mutate(
    variable = factor(variable)
  )




Then, run the following code to show the default contrast matrix that R would use if we used strategy as a predictor right now:

contrasts(heartrate$strategy)

Write down: What contrast coding scheme does this contrast matrix represent?




 Solution 


Solution 3. 

heartrate <- heartrate |>
  mutate(
    strategy = factor(strategy)
  )


contrasts(heartrate$strategy)

           Cough DeepBreath
CloseEyes      0          0
Cough          1          0
DeepBreath     0          1


This contrast coding scheme is treatment coding, which we got to know last week.
By default, R will always treatment-code a categorical predictor unless we tell it otherwise.





Question 4


Apply sum coding to the strategy variable using the function contr.sum().

🗂️ See Sum coding > Define sum coding flash card.

After using contr.sum(), copy and run the following code to give the dummy variables—the columns of the contrast matrix—more useful names that tell you which level is coded as 1 in each variable. You don’t need to know what all the bits of this code mean (unless you want to!).

dimnames(contrasts(heartrate$strategy))[[2]] <- c('CloseEyes', 'Cough')

Finally, generate the contrast matrix for strategy again. Verify that it looks the way you’d expect: do the column names match up with the values labelled 1 in each dummy variable?




 Solution 


Solution 4. 

contrasts(heartrate$strategy) <- contr.sum(3)
contrasts(heartrate$strategy)

           [,1] [,2]
CloseEyes     1    0
Cough         0    1
DeepBreath   -1   -1


For the first dummy variable, CloseEyes is coded as 1, and for the second, it’s Cough. So:

dimnames(contrasts(heartrate$strategy))[[2]] <- c('CloseEyes', 'Cough')

Sense check:

contrasts(heartrate$strategy)

           CloseEyes Cough
CloseEyes          1     0
Cough              0     1
DeepBreath        -1    -1


Good!





Think ahead to model interpretation


Question 5


This is a conceptual/interpretation question—no coding needed.
The model we fit later will have two coefficients which correspond to the strategy variable: strategyCloseEyes and strategyCough. (We know this because there are two columns in the contrast matrix we generated above, and two columns \(\rightarrow\) two dummy variables \(\rightarrow\) two coefficients.)
For each of these two sum-coded slope coefficients, write a brief sentence that describes what each coefficient will mean/represent.
Decide: Which one of those coefficients will help you address the research question?

🗂️ See Sum coding > Model fit and interpretation flash card.





 Solution 


Solution 5. 

strategyCloseEyes: Estimated heart rate when strategy = CloseEyes minus the grand mean heart rate.
strategyCough: Estimated heart rate when strategy = Cough minus the grand mean heart rate.

Well, those are the interpretations if our model were just hr ~ strategy, without controlling for anx!
In a model that does include anx as a covariate, hr ~ strategy + anx, the interpretations become:

strategyCloseEyes: Estimated heart rate when strategy = CloseEyes minus the grand mean heart rate, holding anxiety constant.
strategyCough: Estimated heart rate when strategy = Cough minus the grand mean heart rate, holding anxiety constant.

Now, for the question of which coefficient addresses the RQ. Let’s remind ourselves of the research question: Controlling for people’s pre-existing anxiety levels, is coughing before a lie detector test significantly associated with a lower-than-average heart rate during the test?

The coefficient that will let us address this RQ is strategyCough, which looks exactly at what we want to know: the difference between the heart rate after coughing and the overall average (grand mean) heart rate, holding anxiety constant (and thus controlling for anxiety).






Question 6


This is a conceptual/interpretation question—no coding needed.
The RQ specifies that we must control for people’s pre-existing anxiety levels, which are contained in the continuous numeric variable anx. Therefore, we’ll include anx as a predictor in our model, and we’ll get a coefficient estimate for anx.
Think back to Block 1 and write a brief sentence about what the anx coefficient will mean/represent.

🗂️ See Multiple regression flash card.





 Solution 


Solution 6. Recall that anx has been z-scored, so anx = 0 represents mean anxiety, and anx = 1 represents one SD above the mean.
anx: Holding strategy constant (you can think of this as averaging over all strategies), how much the average heart rate is estimated to increase/decrease when anx increases by one SD.





Question 7


Write out the mathematical formulation of the model we will fit.
Hint: Your model should have three predictors. You can revisit the last couple questions to identify what the predictors should be.

🗂️ See Sum coding > Mathematical model formulation flash card.





 Solution 


Solution 7. \[
\text{heart rate} = \beta_0 +
(\beta_1 \cdot \text{strategy}_\text{CloseEyes}) +
(\beta_2 \cdot \text{strategy}_\text{Cough}) +
(\beta_3 \cdot \text{anx}) +
\epsilon
\]





Fit and interpret the model


Question 8


Fit this linear model in R and name it hr_mdl.
Display the model summary.

🗂️ See Sum coding > Model fit and interpretation flash card.





 Solution 


Solution 8. 

hr_mdl <- lm(hr ~ strategy + anx, data = heartrate)
summary(hr_mdl)


Call:
lm(formula = hr ~ strategy + anx, data = heartrate)

Residuals:

-8.7146 -3.4269 -0.3907  3.0082 11.5010 

Coefficients:
                  Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)        53.9153     0.4897 110.103  < 2e-16 ***
strategyCloseEyes   3.0337     0.7769   3.905 0.000165 ***
strategyCough      -0.8445     0.6502  -1.299 0.196767    
anx                 3.3982     0.7432   4.573 1.29e-05 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 4.567 on 108 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.1749,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.152

Question 9


This is a conceptual/interpretation question—no coding needed.
Write a sentence for each coefficient estimated by the model to interpret/explain what it means.
Bonus: Try to describe in your own words why the intercept means something different for treatment coding and for sum coding.

🗂️ See Sum coding > Model fit and interpretation flash card.

Then, write one sentence that answers the RQ.
Bonus: in the RQ sentence, report the relevant coefficient using APA formatting.

🗂️ See Resources > APA formatting for regression coefficients flash card.





 Solution 


Solution 9. 

(Intercept):

For people with average anxiety, the grand mean heart rate is estimated to be 53.92 bpm.

strategyCloseEyes:

Holding anxiety constant, closing one’s eyes before the lie detector test is associated with an increase of 3.03 bpm compared to the grand mean bpm.

strategyCough:

Holding anxiety constant, coughing before the lie detector test is associated with a decrease of 0.84 bpm compared to the grand mean bpm.

anx:

Holding calming strategy constant, somebody with anxiety one SD above the mean is estimated to have a heart rate 3.40 bpm above the grand mean.


(Remember to mention the units too! You always want to write “[…] estimated to be 53.02 bpm”, not just “estimated to be 53.92.”)

To report a coefficient in APA format, we need to know its 95% CI.

confint(hr_mdl) |> round(2)

                  2.5 % 97.5 %
(Intercept)       52.94  54.89
strategyCloseEyes  1.49   4.57
strategyCough     -2.13   0.44
anx                1.93   4.87


The coefficient that’s relevant for the RQ is strategyCough, so we’ll focus on that one in this sentence which addresses the RQ:
When controlling for anxiety, coughing before a lie detector test is not significantly associated with a lower-than-average heart rate during the test (\(b\) = 0.84, 95% CI [–2.13, 0.44], \(p\) = .197).





Choosing coding schemes for different RQs


Question 10


This is a conceptual/interpretation question—no coding needed.
When you want to use a categorical predictor, you need to choose between treatment coding or sum coding. How do you choose? Based on which coding scheme will let you address your specific RQ best.
Here are five RQs. Based on the phrasing of each one, write down which contrast coding scheme you would use, and also explain why you chose that one. And if you choose treatment coding, also write down your choice of reference level.

Do schoolchildren learn better when their classroom contains natural light compared to artificial light?
What kind of background sound is associated with people spending more money in restaurants: no music, pop music, or classical music?
Is life satisfaction in London lower than the average life satisfaction across UK cities?
Do students in Psychology spend more time studying compared to the average study time across Philosophy, Psychology, and LEL?
In a Stroop task, do neurotypical people perform worse than autistic people?






 Solution 


Solution 10. In general, if your RQ asks you to compare one level of a categorical variable with another level, you should use treatment coding. One of the levels involved in the comparison must be the reference level.

If the variable contains a “baseline” or “default” or “general” level, that should basically always be the reference level.
Otherwise, there’s no specific right answer.
I generally choose the reference level that will make the slope coefficient have the same sign (positive or negative) as the direction of the association in the research question. Examples in (1) and (5) below.

And if your RQ asks you to compare one level of a categorical variable with the average of that variable, then you want sum coding. Make sure that the level involved in the comparison is not your “dropped level”, the one coded as –1.


Do schoolchildren learn better when their classroom contains natural light compared to artificial light?


The RQ asks about a direct comparison between two levels of a predictor, so we want treatment coding.
A good reference level: artificial light, so that the slope coefficient tells us how learning is different given natural light. (Either response is OK here though!)



What kind of background sound is associated with people spending more money in restaurants: no music, pop music, or classical music?


The RQ asks about a direct comparison between two levels of a predictor, so we want treatment coding.
A good reference level: no music, because it’s a natural baseline to compare different kinds of music to.




Is life satisfaction in London lower than the average life satisfaction across different UK cities?



The RQ asks about comparing a particular level (London) of a predictor to the average across all levels (all UK cities), so we want sum coding.



Do students in Psychology spend more time studying compared to the average study time across Philosophy, Psychology, and LEL?


The RQ asks about comparing a particular level (Psychology) of a predictor to the average across all levels (all subject areas in PPLS), so we want sum coding.



In a Stroop task, do neurotypical people perform worse than autistic people?


The RQ asks about a direct comparison between two levels of a predictor, so we want treatment coding.
A good reference level: autistic, so that the slope coefficient tells us how performance is different for neurotypical people. (Either response is OK here though!)

text:
This week, you’ll bootstrap some coefficient estimates for last week’s model.
There’s relatively little new coding this week, so if you have extra time after running through the exercises, why not start putting together some study materials? Your future self will thank you :) We give some recommendations in Q6 below.






NoteGet set up




Open RStudio.
Create a new .Rmd file for this week’s exercises.
Save it somewhere you can find it again.
Give it a clear name (for example, dapr2_lab09.Rmd).
In the first code chunk, load the packages you’ll need this week (and install them if you don’t have them already):

tidyverse
car






Research question (RQ): Is there an association between wellbeing and time spent outdoors, when controlling for the effect that social interaction has on wellbeing?
Data dictionary:








variable
description




age
Age in years of respondent


outdoor_time
Self report estimated number of hours per week spent outdoors


social_int
Self report estimated number of social interactions per week (both online and in-person)


routine
Binary 1=Yes/0=No response to the question 'Do you follow a daily routine throughout the week?'


wellbeing
Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Wellbeing Scale (WEMWBS), a self-report measure of mental health and wellbeing. The scale is scored by summing responses to each item, with items answered on a 1 to 5 Likert scale. The minimum scale score is 14 and the maximum is 70


location
Location of primary residence (City, Suburb, Rural)


steps_k
Average weekly number of steps in thousands (as given by activity tracker if available)













NoteMore detail about this dataset





From the Edinburgh & Lothians, 100 city/suburb residences and 100 rural residences were chosen at random and contacted to participate in the study. The Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Wellbeing Scale (WEMWBS) was used to measure mental health and wellbeing.
Participants filled out a questionnaire including items concerning: estimated average number of hours spent outdoors each week, estimated average number of social interactions each week (whether on-line or in-person), whether a daily routine is followed (yes/no). For those respondents who had an activity tracker app or smart watch, they were asked to provide their average weekly number of steps.





Set up data and model


Question 1


We recommend that you copy and paste code that you wrote last week in Lab 08 for this question.
Read in the data from https://uoepsy.github.io/data/wellbeing_rural.csv and store it in a variable named mwdata (“mw” stands for “mental wellbeing”).
Fit the linear model represented by the mathematical model formulation below and (unlike Lab 03!) name the result m1.
\[
\text{wellbeing} = \beta_0 +
(\beta_1 \cdot \text{outdoor\_time}) +
(\beta_2 \cdot \text{social\_int}) +
\epsilon
\]




 Solution 


Solution 1. 

mwdata <- read_csv("https://uoepsy.github.io/data/wellbeing_rural.csv")
m1     <- lm(wellbeing ~ outdoor_time + social_int, data = mwdata)






Question 2


This is a conceptual/interpretation question—no coding needed.
Here’s a plot from last week’s lab that illustrates a problem with this model’s residuals:

plot(m1, which = 1)








From memory, do your best to write down:

what assumption this plot is checking,
what each point represents, and
what the problem is with the data in this plot.

After you’ve made a good-faith effort to respond to each point from memory, you can revisit last week’s lab/notes/flash cards to complete your responses.




 Solution 


Solution 2. 

This is a residuals-vs-fitted plot, and it’s used to visually assess the assumption of equal variance of errors.
Each point represents one observation from our dataset: specifically, its residual (y axis) and its model-fitted/model-predicted outcome value (x axis).
The problem is that these data points appear to build a fan/funnel/cone shape, where the vertical spread is much smaller at one end of the x axis compared to the other. This pattern indicates unequal variance, and it means we can’t totally trust the model’s estimates of variability, because they won’t apply equally to the whole dataset, and we also can’t totally trust the model’s predicted outcome values, because they’ll be much more accurate when they are small (toward the left side of the plot) and much less accurate when they are large (toward the right side of the plot).






Bootstrap


Question 3


One way to get around the suspicious residuals in the plot above is to bootstrap our linear model’s estimates.
Quick explanation: Why does bootstrapping work? By bootstrapping the model—that is, by fitting the model on a different subset of our data each time—we will end up with a distribution of sampled values for each model coefficient. The mean of that distribution is our coefficient estimate, and the standard deviation of that distribution is our coefficient’s standard error.
Thus bootstrapping gives us a different way to calculate the standard error of our observation, a way that doesn’t rely on the model’s own variability estimates. This is good, because we want to avoid the model’s variability estimates. Why? Because, as the plot above shows, they are not equal across the whole range of the fitted values, so any model-based estimates aren’t going to be entirely trustworthy.
So: using the function Boot(), bootstrap 1000 samples based on the model m1. Name the output m1_boot.






TipCode hint





Replace the ... in the code below with the appropriate values.

... <- Boot(..., R = ...)





🗂️ See Bootstrapping flash card.





 Solution 


Solution 3. 

m1_boot <- Boot(m1, R = 1000)






Question 4


Copy and run the following line of code.

summary(m1_boot)

Write down for yourself:

Which column of the output represents the coefficent estimate?
Which the column of the output represents the standard error (i.e., the standard deviation of the sampling distribution)?


🗂️ See Bootstrapping flash card.





 Solution 


Solution 4. 

summary(m1_boot)


Number of bootstrap replications R = 1000 
             original    bootBias   bootSE  bootMed
(Intercept)  28.62018  3.9198e-02 1.517059 28.67554
outdoor_time  0.19909  2.7539e-05 0.053494  0.20005
social_int    0.33488 -2.4519e-03 0.094052  0.33157



original is the column containing the coefficient estimate.
bootSE is the column containing the bootstrapped standard error.






Question 5


Using the function confint(), find the 95% CIs for each coefficient estimate.
Write down: Can we reject the H0 (at \(\alpha\) = .05) that each coefficient is equal to zero?

🗂️ See Bootstrapping flash card.





 Solution 


Solution 5. 

confint(m1_boot)

Bootstrap bca confidence intervals

                  2.5 %     97.5 %
(Intercept)  25.3587138 31.3027688
outdoor_time  0.0902265  0.3016418
social_int    0.1470745  0.5330718


None of these 95% CIs contain zero, so for all three coefficients, we can reject the H0 at \(\alpha\) = .05.





Develop study materials/strategies


Question 6


If you reach this point and still have a bit of time to dedicate to DAPR this week, we’d recommend that you start thinking about study/revision materials and strategies.
It’s true that report and exam season is still far away, but it’s good to start these things early. Your learning will develop best through little bits of continuous effort. So the more prep you do now, the more your understanding will grow over time.
Here are some of Elizabeth’s favourite learning strategies (note that it’s the process here that will help you learn, much more than just getting an end product):

Mind mapping: Create visual representations of how concepts are connected. You could start a mind map now and keep updating it as the course goes on.
Flash cards (and other active recall methods): Testing yourself using active recall now will train your brain in retrieving key information, so that it’s there when you need it later.

If you like using physical flash cards, try the Leitner system, a system that adds in spaced repetition to help build your long-term memory.

The Feynman technique: Teach or explain an idea as simply as you can. Wherever you’re not sure what to say or how to explain something, brush up on those areas and try again.

Artemis adds that you can also do this explanation method in groups, if you want to mix solo and group study! For example, you might each prep individually and then get together to explain key concepts to one another.
If you don’t know where to start, here are some important questions that you could try to develop an explanation for (again, it’s your process of developing the explanation that’s key, not the actual explanation):

For any intercept in any model, what’s the most general way to describe what it means?
For any slope in any simple regression model (that is, a model with one predictor), what’s the most general way to describe what it means?
For any slope in any multiple regression model (that is, a model with two or more predictors), what’s the most general way to describe what it means?
Why is it important to know what the value zero represents for any predictor?
What is the basic reasoning process / logic of null hypothesis significance testing?
